Plus, is Anthropic misanthropic?

Ford vs. Ferrari

 

“Investing should be more like watching paint dry or watching grass grow,” said Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Samuelson. “If you want excitement, take $800 and go to Las Vegas.”

 

We’re in a golden age for people who’ve embraced Samuelson’s advice. The largest fund managers compete over hundredths of a percentage point in expenses for running giant index funds. They’re the Fords of the investing business.

 

Then there are the Ferraris. Firms that could never get big enough to compete purely on cost have launched thousands of funds featuring income-boosting gimmicks or media-savvy stock pickers. They’re prone to crashing, but the survivors make lots of money for the managers.

 

Dave Nadig of ETF.com did the math by calculating different fund companies’ revenue per dollar of assets under management. At the bottom of the expense heap is index fund Pioneer Vanguard, owner of the first trillion-dollar ETF, at just four hundredths of a percent.

 
 
 
 

At the opposite extreme is YieldMax, which rakes in about 27 times as much per dollar. Its funds use derivatives to achieve “distribution yields” of 60% or more. YieldMax’s oldest fund, which has since tweaked its strategy, pays out lots of cash by tracking Tesla. But, since its launch less than four years ago, just buying Tesla stock outright would have made an investor 66 percentage points more of total return.

 

Leveraged ETFs offer even gaudier results over short periods, and stinging losses too. Sometimes funds that are long and short an index both lose money. Direxion, a pioneer of the category, makes about 21 times Vanguard’s revenue per dollar managed.

 

Another fund family that collects an impressive amount by that measure is active manager ARK Invest. Chief Executive and Chief Investment Officer Cathie Wood has been ubiquitous in financial media since a hot streak early this decade.

 

But taking in about 18 times Vanguard’s revenue hasn’t paid for superior performance. Wood, who claims to be “benchmark agnostic,” has struggled in her main tech-heavy fund, Ark Innovation ETF, in the past five years. It has trailed a Nasdaq-100 index ETF by more than 130 percentage points. Morningstar named the fund number one for shareholder wealth destruction.

 

Wood predicted in 2022 that her portfolio would compound at 50% annually over many years—not a promise, but emotional catnip for investors intent on getting rich in a hurry.

 

The underlying funds differ, but the common theme of complex or active ETFs is a fast track to investing success. Don’t just look under the hood—check out the price tag.
